meta.title: 171: To reward or not to reward your ADHD kid?
meta.description:
In this episode I break down the fears we all have about giving our ADHD kids REWARDS for their behavior. 

I share WHY rewards help to motivate your ADHD child, but HOW to use them more effectively and strategically. 

This will answer the bribery questions, the “will I reward my child forever” question, and will my child only do things if I give them stuff question. :) 

🚨FIRST EVER ADHD BEHAVIOR BLUEPRINT 🚨LIVE EVENT IS HAPPENING!!🚨

You’re having the same power struggle over the tasks that HAVE to get done. Homework, teeth brushing, putting ONE piece of clothing away, bedtime… heaven forbid you ALSO ask that they speak kindly during this process. 🤯

The level of overwhelm, dysregulation, and frustration you’re living with day to day is real and it’s unfair. 🙅🏼‍♀️This is NOT what you pictured parenting to look like, and this version of you as a parent, is not aligning with your values. 

You want to be a kind, accepting, patient person but you end up snapping or getting into your ADHD kid’s feelings with them.

🎉But that all changes now! 🎉

You’re going to be able to stop walking on eggshells, stop feeling utterly defeated and like you’re making all the wrong choices, and ACTUALLY KNOW how you and your child can get through both transitions and all the everyday “must do tasks” without yet another fight! AND, you don’t need to repeat yourself to the point of yelling!

Imagine feeling grounded and proud of yourself for navigating the day with regulation instead of multiple yelling matches. 

There are many ADHD strategies out there, but after working exclusively with severe high conflict families, I’ve filtered out what doesn’t work for ADHD kids (*cough gentle parenting) and combined my education, research & lived experience into the core A.B.L.E. Method. 

You do not need to have the same battle every day. It starts with regulation, a plan, some practice reps, and a lot of reinforcement. Not sure how that looks in real life? Don’t worry! I’ve got your back in a 2 day live event (well on zoom but with me😂) where we go over YOUR repeated battle and we BUILD YOUR PLAN so all you have to do is execute it!

January 9th & 10th, 2027 (9am-11am PST both days) *Recorded for those who can’t attend live. 

No more second guessing, no more confusion, just a proven strategy to support your power struggle. 

This live event IS FREE to all existing ResponseABLE Community members! 

So come to a free masterclass or just JOIN THE PROGRAM, and get ready to have me walk side by side with you as we map out your 2027 behavior plan so you can actually start enjoying time with your ADHD child again! 

FREE masterclass: https://calendly.com/responseableparenting/adhd-masterclass

JOIN here: https://www.responseableparenting.com/join 

Live event dates: Jan 9-10th. 2 hours on Saturday / 2 hours on Sunday morning (9-11am PST).  We take your chronic fight and your goal and we break down every step that needs to happen to make that goal a reality! 

MINI COURSE:

Grab my 39 minute video / workbook combo where you will learn exactly why you feel so awful in these moments with your ADHD kid AND you’ll learn the steps necessary to get out of the heat of the moment and stop reacting so quickly to the same repetitive fight. 

You can grab Before You Lose It right here! https://responseable-community.circle.so/checkout/gap 

FREE RESOURCES!

Tired of repeating yourself over the same behaviors? Try this VALUES DECK OF CARDS! You can customize the cards to your family values and instead of dishing out yet another punishment, you can instill positive consequences through the actions on the back!
https://responseableparenting.kit.com/cards

Get the cheat codes to “stack” regulation practices throughout your day! No time to meditate? No problem. Grab this simple system and add ZERO time to your day!
https://responseableparenting.kit.com/zero

Book a call with me to connect on areas of your parenting that are causing pain, struggle, or frustration. https://calendly.com/responseableparenting/call

summary.one_liner: Becky Jennings explains why reward systems, when used correctly, help motivate ADHD kids by jumpstarting their underactive dopamine reward centers.
summary.summary:
Becky Jennings addresses a common parenting dilemma: whether rewarding ADHD kids for basic tasks counts as bribery or undermines internal motivation. She explains the neuroscience behind ADHD, noting that these kids' dopamine reward centers are quieter and less responsive to delayed gratification, so a reward promised too far in the future loses its motivating power through what researchers call steep discounting.

She describes rewards as jumper cables for a car with a weak starter: they are needed to get the engine (motivation) running, not as permanent payment for behavior. Small, immediate, specific rewards like praise, fake money, or stickers are far more effective than big delayed prizes, and they should be faded out over time as the child builds the underlying skill through repeated practice and simulation.

Jennings distinguishes true rewards from bribery. Bribery is giving in during a meltdown just to stop bad behavior in the moment, whereas a proper reward system is planned and agreed upon in advance, during a calm period, so the child knows exactly what behavior earns what reward. She references Alan Kazdin's research from the Yale Parenting Center as evidence supporting this micro-reward, practice-and-praise approach for aggressive, oppositional, and defiant behaviors often seen alongside ADHD.

She stresses that rewards should never be taken away as punishment, and that children should help co-create their own reward systems to increase buy-in. The episode closes with a promotion for her parenting program and an upcoming live masterclass and two-day event focused on building personalized behavior plans, available to those who join before November 30th.
takeaways: ADHD brains have a quieter reward center and need immediate dopamine triggers rather than relying on the anticipation of a future reward.
About 78% of kids with combined type ADHD show steep discounting, meaning rewards lose value the longer they have to wait for them.
Boring, non-preferred tasks don't light up the ADHD reward center, so kids may unconsciously create conflict to generate the stimulation needed to act.
Small, immediate, frequent, and specific rewards like verbal praise or fake money are more effective than big delayed prizes.
True rewards are planned in advance and agreed upon ahead of time, unlike bribery which is given reactively during a meltdown to stop bad behavior.
Rewards should be gradually faded out as the child builds skill, acting as a temporary jumpstart rather than a permanent transaction.
Earned rewards should never be taken away as punishment, since this undermines the child's trust that good behavior is reliably recognized.
Involving the child in co-creating their own reward system increases their buy-in and investment in the behavior plan.
Specific praise naming the exact positive behavior is more effective than vague praise like 'good job,' which can cause confusion or anxiety.
